groups.name: First win
groups.intro: A dozen short, famous stories with almost no argument to follow. Learn to read one step at a time and see where a story begins and ends.

groups.name: Short stories
groups.intro: More short stories, a few minutes each, from all over Shas. They build your ear for the Gemara's Aramaic and its way of telling a story.

groups.name: Getting hooked
groups.intro: Longer stories with a question at their heart. Watch how the Gemara sets up a puzzle and then resolves it.

groups.name: Big ideas
groups.intro: Teachings rather than stories: a sage makes a claim and proves it from a verse. Learn to follow a proof and see how one teaching leads to the next.

groups.name: Harder
groups.intro: Long stories across two or three amudim, including the Purim story in six parts. Practise keeping track of many people and scenes.

groups.name: First halachic sugyos
groups.intro: Short halachic passages, often the opening Mishnah of a masechta. Learn the basic moves: a Mishnah, a question, an answer, a proof.

groups.name: Following a halachic argument
groups.intro: Classic sugyos where the Gemara builds an argument step by step, with challenges, answers and a conclusion.

items.title: Honi and the carob tree
items.summary: All his life Honi wondered how anyone could sleep for seventy years. One day he meets a man planting a carob tree that will only bear fruit in seventy years, and then Honi himself falls asleep for seventy years. He wakes to find the man's grandson eating its fruit, and nobody believes who he is. Start there, then go back for the story of him drawing a circle and refusing to move until it rains.

items.title: Rabbi Yosi prays in the ruins and meets Eliyahu
items.summary: Rabbi Yosi tells how he went into a ruin of Jerusalem to pray, and Eliyahu guarded the doorway until he finished. Eliyahu tells him he should have prayed on the road with a short prayer, and Rabbi Yosi learns three lessons. Then Eliyahu asks what he heard there: a heavenly voice cooing like a dove, 'Woe, that I destroyed My house and exiled My children.' Eliyahu says it says this three times every day, and when Israel answers 'May His great name be blessed' in shul, God nods and says, 'Happy is the king who is praised like this in his house.'

items.title: Suffering out of love
items.summary: Rava teaches that when suffering comes, a person should first examine his deeds, then ask if he neglected Torah study, and if he finds neither, these are 'sufferings of love', because God rebukes the one He loves. If he accepts them with love, his reward is children, long life, and learning that stays with him. Two Amoraim argue about which suffering counts as 'of love', and Rabbi Yochanan says both kinds do. It ends with Reish Lakish: just as salt sweetens meat, suffering cleanses all of a person's sins.

items.title: Why did earlier generations get miracles?
items.summary: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why miracles happened for earlier generations and not for them, even though they learn more: in Rav Yehuda's time they learned only Nezikin, yet when Rav Yehuda took off one shoe, rain came, while we cry out and no one notices. Abaye answers: the earlier generations were ready to give up their lives to sanctify God's name, and we are not. The example is Rav Adda bar Ahava, who tore a forbidden garment off a woman in the market thinking she was Jewish. She was not, and he was fined 400 zuz; her name was Matun, and he said, 'Matun, matun is worth 400 zuz.'
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. items.title: Moshe's daring prayer after the golden calf: 'Leave Me alone'
items.summary: After the golden calf, God tells Moshe 'Go down', meaning: step down from your greatness, and Moshe loses the strength to speak. But when God says 'Leave Me alone, and I will destroy them', Moshe understands that it depends on him, and he prays hard for mercy, like the friend of a king who stands up and saves the king's son. Rabbi Abahu says Moshe grabbed hold of God, like a man grabbing his friend's garment, and said he would not let go until God forgave them. Moshe also argues against God's offer to make a great nation from him: if a three-legged chair cannot stand before God's anger, how could a one-legged one, and he would be ashamed before the Avos.

items.title: The pious man who would not stop his prayer for an officer
items.summary: A pious man was praying on the road when an officer greeted him; he did not answer, and the officer waited until he finished. The officer angrily asked why he had risked his life. The pious man answered: if you stood before a human king and a friend greeted you, would you answer him? You would lose your head. How much more so when I stand before the King of kings, who lives forever. The officer was appeased, and the pious man went home in peace.

items.title: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa: 'I know if my prayer is fluent'
items.summary: Rabban Gamliel's son falls ill, and he sends two scholars to Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, who goes up to the attic and prays. He comes down and tells them the fever has left the boy. 'Are you a prophet?' 'No, but I have a tradition: if my prayer flows smoothly, I know it was accepted.' They write down the time, and Rabban Gamliel confirms the fever left at that exact moment. In a second story Rabbi Chanina's prayer heals Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's son, who explains to his wife that Chanina is like a servant before the King, while he is like a minister.

items.title: Og's mountain and the places of miracles
items.summary: A beraisa lists places where one who sees them must thank God: the crossings of the sea, the Jordan and the Arnon streams, the hailstones at Beis Choron, the rock Og wanted to throw on Israel, the rock Moshe sat on, Lot's wife, and the sunken wall of Jericho. The Gemara tells the story behind each. Hidden Amorites at the Arnon were crushed when the mountains closed together. Og uprooted a mountain three parsa'os wide to throw on Israel's camp, but God sent insects that bored through it, it fell onto his neck, his teeth grew so he could not pull it off, and Moshe struck him on the ankle and killed him. It ends by explaining the blessings over Lot and his wife and why Jericho's wall sank.

items.title: Rabbi Akiva's donkey, rooster and lamp: 'Everything God does is for the good'
items.summary: Rav Huna teaches that a person should always be used to saying, 'Everything the Merciful One does is for the good', as Rabbi Akiva did. Turned away from a town with no place to stay, he slept in a field; the wind blew out his lamp, a cat ate his rooster and a lion ate his donkey, and each time he said, 'It is for the good.' That very night an army captured the town. He said: 'Didn't I tell you? Everything God does is all for the good.'

items.title: Chananya ben Chizkiya saves the book of Yechezkel
items.summary: Chananya ben Chizkiya and his group wrote Megillas Taanis, the record of the days of rescue, because they cherished the memory of the troubles. Then Rav says this man should be remembered for good: without him the book of Yechezkel would have been hidden away, because its words seemed to contradict the Torah. They brought him three hundred jars of oil, and he sat in his attic and explained it.

items.title: Chanukah lights versus Shabbos lights: which comes first?
items.summary: Rava says it is obvious that the Shabbos light of the house comes before a Chanukah light, and before Kiddush, because it brings peace in the home. Then he asks: between a Chanukah light and Kiddush, which comes first? Kiddush is more frequent, but the Chanukah light publicizes the miracle, and he decides the Chanukah light wins. Then Rav Huna teaches that one who regularly lights candles will have sons who are Torah scholars, with stories of sages who saw homes with many lights, and Rav Yosef's wife learns to light neither too early nor too late.

items.title: God's seal is truth: the marks on the foreheads
items.summary: Rabbi Zeira tells Rabbi Simon to rebuke the Reish Galusa's household even if they will not listen, and explains with a lesson from Yechezkel. God told Gavriel to mark the righteous of Jerusalem with a letter tav in ink so the destroying angels would spare them, and the wicked with a tav in blood. The Attribute of Justice argued that the righteous could have protested and did not; God answered it would not have helped, and Justice replied, 'You knew that, but did they?' So the punishment began with the righteous, the only time a good decree from God was reversed. The Gemara then asks why the letter tav, and Reish Lakish answers that tav ends God's seal, which is emes, truth.

items.title: Moshe argues with the angels: 'Were you slaves in Egypt?'
items.summary: When Moshe went up to receive the Torah, the angels protested: why give a treasure hidden since before Creation to flesh and blood? God told Moshe to answer them while holding on to His Throne. Moshe asked what the Torah says: 'I took you out of Egypt': were you slaves to Pharaoh? 'Keep Shabbos': do you work? 'Honor your parents': do you have parents? 'Do not murder or steal': is there jealousy or an evil inclination among you? The angels agreed with God, each one became Moshe's friend and gave him a gift, and even the Angel of Death told him a secret.

items.title: The children's alef-beis lessons
items.summary: The Rabbis tell Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that young children came to the study hall and said things not heard even in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun: lessons from the letters. Alef-beis means 'learn wisdom'; gimmel reaches toward dalet because a giver runs after the poor, and dalet turns its face away so the gift is given privately. Kuf (holy) turns away from reish (wicked), but its open leg lets one who repents come back in. The letters of sheker (falsehood) are close together and stand on one leg, while the letters of emes (truth) are far apart and stand firm: falsehood is common, but only truth lasts.

items.title: Yosef who honored Shabbos and the pearl in the fish
items.summary: Yosef, known as 'the one who honors Shabbos', lived near a rich non-Jew whom astrologers warned that Yosef would end up with all his property. The man sold everything for one pearl and put it in his hat, but the wind blew it into a river and a fish swallowed it. The fish was brought to market late on Friday, and Yosef, who always bought for Shabbos, bought it, found the pearl, and sold it for thirteen containers of gold coins. An old man said: 'Whoever lends to Shabbos, Shabbos repays him.' Then Rebbi is told that the rich in other lands earn their wealth by honoring Shabbos, and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba tells of a rich man in Laodicea who had always saved his best animals for Shabbos.

items.title: The two angels who walk you home on Friday night
items.summary: Whoever says Vayechulu on Friday night becomes a partner with God in Creation, and the two angels who escort him put their hands on his head and say, 'Your sin is removed.' Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda teaches that two angels, one good and one bad, walk a person home from shul on Friday night. If the lamp is lit, the table set and the bed made, the good angel says, 'May it be like this next Shabbos', and the bad angel must answer Amen. If not, the bad angel says it, and the good angel must answer Amen.

items.title: Hospitality is greater than greeting the Shechinah; judging others favorably
items.summary: Rav says welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence, learned from Avraham, who asked God to wait while he turned to his guests. Rabbi Yochanan lists six mitzvos whose fruits we enjoy in this world, among them welcoming guests and judging others favorably. The Gemara then tells three stories of people who saw something suspicious and assumed the best: a worker whose employer said he had nothing to pay him, students of a pious man who ransomed a captive girl, and Rabbi Yehoshua's students when he visited a Roman noblewoman. Each time the one judged says, 'That is exactly what happened; as you judged me favorably, may God judge you favorably.'

items.title: 'Repent one day before your death' and the king's banquet
items.summary: Rabbi Eliezer taught: repent one day before your death. His students asked how anyone knows when he will die. He answered: all the more so, repent today, since you might die tomorrow, and your whole life will be spent in repentance. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's parable: a king invited his servants to a feast without saying when. The wise dressed up and waited at the palace door, while the foolish went to work; when the king suddenly called, the ready ones sat and ate, and the unready, in Rabbi Meir's version, sat hungry and thirsty.

items.title: There is no mazal for Israel: Rabbi Akiva's daughter and the snake
items.summary: Rabbi Chanina says the stars affect Jews too, but Rabbi Yochanan and Rav say there is no mazal for Israel, and God tells Avraham to step outside his astrology. Stories prove it: a man an astrologer said would die of a snakebite came back alive after quietly sparing a poor man shame, and Rabbi Akiva's daughter, predicted to die of a snakebite on her wedding day, killed the snake with her hairpin without knowing it after giving her food to a poor man. Each time the lesson was 'charity saves from death' itself. Last, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's mother kept his head covered after astrologers said he would be a thief; the one time his cloak slipped off, he climbed a palm tree and bit off a cluster of dates.

items.title: An alleyway entrance more than twenty amos high
items.summary: The Mishnah: an alleyway whose entrance is higher than twenty amos must be lowered, but Rabbi Yehuda says it need not be; one wider than ten amos must be narrowed unless it has the shape of a doorway. The Gemara compares the rule of a sukkah taller than twenty amos and asks why one Mishnah says 'invalid' and the other gives a fix. Rav says the Sages learned the twenty-amah limit from the doorway of the Heichal in the Temple, and Rabbi Yehuda from the taller doorway of the Ulam, and the Gemara works through the verses and challenges. Finally Rav Chisda says a beraisa misled Rav: Rabbi Yehuda really learned from the gateways of kings.

items.title: Rabbi Yehoshua is out-talked by a woman, a girl and a boy
items.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya says only a woman, a girl and a boy ever beat him. An innkeeper over-salted his beans; when he said he had already eaten, she said he should have skipped the bread, and maybe he was leaving some over now because he left nothing the first days. A girl caught him cutting through a field, and when he said it was a trodden path, she answered, 'Robbers like you trod it.' A boy told him one road was 'short and long'; it led to orchards blocking the city, and the boy said, 'Didn't I tell you it was long?' Rabbi Yehoshua kissed him and said, 'Fortunate are you, Israel: all of you are wise, from old to young.'

items.title: How Moshe taught the Torah, and Rabbi Preida who taught one student 400 times
items.summary: A beraisa describes how Moshe taught: he taught Aharon, then Aharon's sons, then the elders, then all the people, and then each teacher repeated it, so everyone heard it four times. From here Rabbi Eliezer learns that a teacher must teach his student four times, and Rabbi Akiva says until the student knows it. Rabbi Preida had a student who needed every lesson 400 times; once the student was distracted and did not get it, and Rabbi Preida taught him another 400 times. A heavenly voice offered Rabbi Preida 400 more years of life or the World to Come for him and his generation; he chose the World to Come, and God said: give him both.

items.title: Learning modesty from the cat
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan says that if the Torah had not been given, we would have learned modesty from the cat, not stealing from the ant, avoiding forbidden relationships from the dove, and proper marital conduct from the rooster, which first wins over its mate. How does the rooster do it? Rav says it promises her a coat reaching down to her feet, and then says, 'May my crest fall off if I have the money and don't buy it for you.'

items.title: Whose blood is redder? Never kill to save yourself
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that a person may use anything to heal himself except idolatry, forbidden relations and bloodshed. The Gemara finds a source for the first two in verses, and asks how we know a person must die rather than murder. The answer is simple logic: a man told Rava that a local ruler ordered him to kill someone or be killed, and Rava told him to let himself be killed, because who says your blood is redder? Maybe the other man's blood is redder.

items.title: Ten things created at twilight before the first Shabbos
items.summary: A baraisa lists ten things created on the first Friday at twilight, among them the well, the manna, the rainbow, the writing and the tool that wrote the Luchos, Moshe's grave, and the mouth of the earth that swallowed the wicked; others add Aharon's staff, the demons and Adam's garment. items.title: Hillel and the Bnei Beseira: Pesach on Shabbos
items.summary: The Mishnah lists which parts of the Pesach offering override Shabbos, and Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva argue over the lesser preparations. The Gemara then tells how the Bnei Beseira forgot whether the Pesach overrides Shabbos, called Hillel, who had studied with Shemaya and Avtalyon, and made him Nasi when he proved it does. Hillel scolded them, then forgot what to do about a knife not brought before Shabbos, and said to watch the people: they came with knives stuck in the lambs' wool and the goats' horns, and Hillel remembered that this was the law he had received.

items.title: Rabbi Akiva's instructions to his son
items.summary: Rabbi Akiva commands his son Rabbi Yehoshua seven things: don't learn at the busy high point of a city, don't live in a city whose leaders are Torah scholars, don't walk into a house suddenly, don't go barefoot, eat early in the morning, make Shabbos like a weekday rather than depend on others, and try to join with someone whose luck is smiling on him. Rav Pappa says to partner with such a person rather than trade with him, but the Gemara concludes that even trading with a blessed person brings blessing.

items.title: Begin with shame, end with praise: how the Seder tells the story
items.summary: The Mishnah says the second cup is poured, the son asks Mah Nishtanah, and the father teaches him according to his understanding, beginning with shame and ending with praise. The Gemara says that if there is no son, the wife or even oneself asks, and Rava and Rav Safra argue over the wording about dipping. Rav says the shame is 'at first our fathers served idols' and Shmuel says 'we were slaves'; when Rav Nachman's servant Daru said a freed slave must thank and praise, Rav Nachman said he had exempted them from Mah Nishtanah and began 'Avadim hayinu'.

items.title: The four New Years
items.summary: The Mishnah lists four New Years: Nisan for kings and festivals, Elul for the animal tithe, Tishrei for years, Shemittah, Yovel, planting and vegetables, and Shevat for trees, with Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel arguing over the first or fifteenth. The Gemara explains that the New Year for kings matters for dating documents, works through a baraisa on how a king's years are counted, and brings Rabbi Yochanan's proof from a verse about Shlomo's reign that kings' years are counted from Nisan.

items.title: The three books opened on Rosh Hashanah
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that three books are opened on Rosh Hashanah: the completely righteous are written and sealed for life at once, the completely wicked for death, and those in the middle hang until Yom Kippur. Two verses are brought as hints. A baraisa then describes three groups on the final Day of Judgment: Beis Shammai say the in-between go down to Gehinnom, cry out and come up, while Beis Hillel say God, 'abundant in kindness', tilts the scale toward kindness.

items.title: Eli's family, and Rabbah and Abaye who lived long through Torah and kindness
items.summary: Can a decree against a community be torn up? The Gemara answers that a decree sworn with an oath cannot: God swore that the sin of Eli’s family would not be atoned through sacrifice or offering. Rava says it can still be atoned through Torah, and Abaye says through Torah and acts of kindness. Rabbah and Abaye were both from Eli's family: Rabbah, who learned Torah, lived forty years, and Abaye, who learned Torah and did kindness, lived sixty. A Jerusalem family whose men died at eighteen was told by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai to learn Torah, and they lived.

items.title: Must you intend to fulfil the mitzvah when you hear the shofar?
items.summary: A ruling was sent that someone forced to eat matzah has fulfilled the mitzvah; Rav Ashi says it means Persians forced him. Rava learns from this that one who blows shofar just for music is also yotzei, so he holds that mitzvos do not need intent. The Gemara challenges him from sources that say 'if he directed his heart', and answers that they mean intent to read or to hear, as when he thought the shofar was just a donkey; a baraisa requiring both blower and listener to have intent is explained as a blower just making barking sounds.

items.title: The Kohen Gadol is separated seven days before Yom Kippur
items.summary: The Mishnah says that seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is moved from his home to a chamber in the Temple and a backup Kohen is prepared; Rabbi Yehudah would even prepare a backup wife, and the Sages say there would be no end to it. The Gemara compares the Kohen who burns the red heifer, explains his chamber and its stone vessels, and asks for the source: Rabbi Yochanan learns it from the seven days of the Mishkan's inauguration, applying 'to do' to the red heifer and 'to atone' to Yom Kippur.

items.title: The race up the ramp and the stabbing in the Temple
items.summary: Kohanim used to race up the altar ramp to win the job of clearing the ashes. Once two were tied, one got ahead, and the other took a knife and stabbed him in the heart. Rabbi Tzadok stood on the steps and asked who should bring the calf for an unsolved killing, and all the people wept; the boy's father came and said the knife was still pure because his son was still convulsing, which shows that purity of vessels mattered more to them than bloodshed. The Gemara asks whether this came before or after the broken-leg incident, and concludes the murder came first and was seen as a freak event until they saw the race itself was dangerous and made a lottery.

items.title: Nikanor's doors
items.summary: Nikanor brought doors for the Temple from Alexandria. A storm threatened to sink the ship, so the sailors threw one door overboard; when they tried to throw the second, Nikanor wrapped himself around it and said to throw him in too, and the sea calmed. When they reached Acco the lost door was sticking out from under the ship. That is why all the Temple gates were later made of gold except Nikanor's.

items.title: Then: the families who would not share their secrets
items.summary: The Mishnah names those remembered with disgrace, including the family of Garmu, who would not teach how to bake the showbread, and the family of Avtinas, who would not teach how to make the incense. The Sages replaced each with craftsmen from Alexandria, who could not match them, and had to bring them back for double wages. Asked why, both families said they feared the skill would be used for idolatry after the Temple fell, and they never used fine bread or perfume at home so no one would suspect them. Later a descendant of Avtinas gave Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri the scroll of spices, and Rabbi Akiva said from now on it is forbidden to speak badly of them.

items.title: After Shimon HaTzaddik died: the signs that stopped
items.summary: During the forty years Shimon HaTzaddik served, the lot for God always came up in the right hand, the red strip turned white, the western lamp kept burning, the altar fire stayed strong, and a small piece of the holy bread filled each Kohen; after him these became uncertain. Shimon HaTzaddik foretold his own death after seeing an old man dressed in black on Yom Kippur. Forty years before the destruction the signs stopped altogether and the Temple doors opened by themselves, until Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rebuked them, saying he knew the Temple would be destroyed.

items.title: The keruvim embracing
items.summary: Rav Ketina says that when the people came up for the festival, the curtain was rolled back to show them the keruvim embracing, and they were told: see how beloved you are before God, like the love of man and woman. The Gemara asks how that could be allowed, answers with the parable of a bride, and discusses whether this was in the first or second Temple. When the nations entered the Sanctuary and saw the keruvim clinging to each other, they paraded them in the market to mock the Jews.

items.title: Shemaya and Avtalyon and the Kohen Gadol
items.summary: When a Kohen Gadol left the Temple after Yom Kippur, everyone followed him, until they saw Shemaya and Avtalyon and followed them instead. When the two came to take leave of him, the Kohen Gadol mocked them as descendants of other nations. They answered: let the descendants of the nations come in peace, since they act like Aharon, and let the son of Aharon not come in peace, since he does not.

items.title: Chillul Hashem and the greatness of teshuvah
items.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya teaches three levels of atonement, each with teshuvah, but desecrating God's name is atoned only by death. Rav, Rabbi Yochanan and others give examples, such as a scholar who doesn't pay the butcher right away, and Abaye explains that a learned person who deals honestly sanctifies God's name while one who doesn't desecrates it. Then a series of teachings on the greatness of teshuvah: it brings healing, reaches the Throne of Glory, overrides a Torah prohibition, brings redemption, turns sins into errors or even merits, lengthens life, and for one person who repents the whole world is forgiven.

items.title: A stolen lulav: a mitzvah that comes through a sin
items.summary: The Mishnah says a stolen or dry lulav is invalid. The Gemara asks why a stolen one is invalid even after the first day, when 'yours' is no longer required, and Rabbi Yochanan answers in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's name that it is a mitzvah that comes through a sin, compared by a verse to a lame offering; Rabbi Yochanan adds the parable of a king who pays the toll so his servants will learn. Shmuel holds a stolen lulav is invalid only on the first day, and Rava explains the Mishnah to fit him.

items.title: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: 'I have seen the people of the upper world, and they are few'
items.summary: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says his merit can free the whole world from judgment, more so with his son Eliezer and with Yosam ben Uziyahu. He also says he has seen the people of the highest level and they are few: if a thousand, he and his son are among them, and if only two, they are he and his son. The Gemara asks how this fits with Rava's eighteen thousand before God, or Abaye's teaching that the world always has at least thirty-six righteous who greet the Shechinah each day, and answers that it depends on how clear their vision is and whether they enter with permission.

items.title: Whoever has not seen the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah…
items.summary: The Mishnah says whoever did not see the celebration of the Water Drawing never saw joy. Golden menorahs lit with wicks from the Kohanim's old clothes lit up every courtyard in Jerusalem, pious men danced with torches, the Levites played on the fifteen steps, and at dawn the Kohanim turned west and declared 'our eyes are to God'. The Gemara adds that whoever did not see the Temple built never saw a beautiful building, meaning Herod's, built of marble that looked like waves of the sea, and the Sages told Herod not to cover it in gold.

items.title: The evil inclination: a mountain to the righteous, a hair to the wicked
items.summary: The Gemara asks what the great mourning in Zechariah's prophecy is for: one view says Mashiach ben Yosef, who is killed, and the other says the evil inclination. Rabbi Yehudah teaches that God will slaughter the evil inclination before everyone; to the righteous it looks like a high mountain and to the wicked like a hair, and both weep, the righteous that they conquered it and the wicked that they could not. Rav Assi adds that the evil inclination starts like a spider's thread and ends like a wagon rope.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Title changed from 'first a hair, then a mountain': in the Gemara the mountain and the hair are how it looks to the righteous and the wicked, and the 'thin then thick' image is Rav Assi's spider thread and wagon rope. Step 3 asks about 'this mourning', meaning the verse quoted just before (52a 1).

items.title: At the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah: Hillel's 'if I am here', and eight torches
items.summary: At the Water Drawing celebration the pious sang 'happy is our youth that did not shame our old age' and the penitents 'happy is our old age that atoned for our youth'. Hillel said 'if I am here, all is here', taught that a person's feet bring him where he is needed (shown in the story of Shlomo's two scribes and the Angel of Death), and told a floating skull that those who drowned others are drowned. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel juggled eight burning torches, other Sages juggled knives, cups and eggs, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya said they hardly slept all festival, only dozing on each other's shoulders.

items.title: Eruv tavshilin: how you may cook on Yom Tov for Shabbos
items.summary: The Mishnah says that when Yom Tov falls on Friday you may not start cooking on Yom Tov for Shabbos, but you may prepare a dish before Yom Tov and rely on it; Beis Shammai require two dishes and Beis Hillel one. Shmuel finds a source in 'Remember the Shabbos', and Rava and Rav Ashi argue whether the reason is to save a good portion for Shabbos or so people learn that one may not cook on Yom Tov for another day. A tanna finds a Torah hint in the manna: 'what you will bake, bake'.

items.title: A person's income is fixed on Rosh Hashanah; Shammai's best animal and Hillel's trust
items.summary: A person's income for the year is fixed between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, except what he spends on Shabbos, Yom Tov and his children's Torah learning: if he spends less he is given less, and if more, more. Shammai ate all week in honor of Shabbos, setting aside any fine animal for Shabbos and swapping it if he found a better one. Hillel had a different way, trusting God 'day by day', and the dispute appears again between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel.

items.title: Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yitzchak: the blessing of the tree
items.summary: As they part, Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak to bless him. Rabbi Yitzchak tells a parable of a hungry, thirsty traveler who rests under a tree with sweet fruit, good shade and a stream. When he leaves, he has nothing to wish the tree that it doesn't already have, so he blesses it that all the saplings planted from it be like it. So too, says Rabbi Yitzchak: you already have Torah, wealth and children, so may your children be like you.

items.title: Wisdom in an ugly vessel: Rabbi Yehoshua and the emperor's daughter
items.summary: Rabbi Oshaya teaches that Torah is like water, wine and milk: they keep only in the plainest containers, and Torah stays only with a humble person. The emperor's daughter mocks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: such beautiful wisdom in such an ugly vessel! He asks why her father keeps his wine in clay jars and suggests gold and silver, and the wine turns sour. When the emperor objects that some handsome people are learned, the answer is that if they were ugly they would be even more learned.

items.title: "Gam zu letovah": Nachum Ish Gamzu
items.summary: Nachum Ish Gamzu is blind, without hands or feet and covered in boils, lying in a shaky house that does not fall until he is carried out. He tells his students he brought it on himself: a poor man died while Nachum delayed feeding him, and Nachum asked for this suffering. He was called Gamzu because whatever happened he said "this too is for the good." Sent with a chest of jewels to the emperor, he finds it filled with earth, says "this too is for the good," and Eliyahu, in disguise, suggests it is Avraham's miraculous earth. It wins a war, Nachum is sent home with honor, and the innkeepers who stole the jewels try the same trick and are killed.

items.title: Eliyahu points out who has a share in the World to Come: the jailer and the jesters
items.summary: Rabbi Beroka asks Eliyahu in the market whether anyone there has a share in the World to Come. Eliyahu points to a man with black shoes and no tzitzis, who turns out to be a jailer who keeps men and women apart, saves Jewish girls from harm, and dresses like a non-Jew so he can warn the Sages of decrees. Then Eliyahu points to two brothers, who explain that they are jesters who cheer up sad people and make peace between people who are fighting.

items.title: Rabbi Yosi of Yokrat: his son, his daughter, his donkey
items.summary: Rabbi Yosi bar Avin leaves his teacher Rabbi Yosi of Yokrat for Rav Ashi, and explains: a man with no mercy on his own son and daughter would have none on me. Rabbi Yosi's son made a fig tree give fruit early to feed his father's hungry workers, and his father said: you troubled your Creator to bring fruit before its time, so you will be taken before your time. When a man peeked at his beautiful daughter, he told her to return to her dust. His donkey went home with its rental fee, refusing to move if the fee was wrong or if sandals were left on it.

items.title: "The whole world is fed for My son Chanina"
items.summary: Every day a heavenly voice says the whole world is fed in Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa's merit, while he lives on a small measure of carobs a week. His wife, ashamed of having nothing to bake, made smoke in her oven every Friday; when a nasty neighbor came to check, the oven was miraculously full of bread. Later he prayed and received a leg of a golden table, but his wife dreamed they would then eat at a table missing a leg in the World to Come, so he prayed and it was taken back, a greater miracle than the first.

items.title: The young kohanim throw the Temple keys to heaven
items.summary: When the first Temple was destroyed, groups of young kohanim went up to the roof of the Sanctuary with its keys and said: since we were not worthy to be faithful treasurers, let the keys be handed to You. They threw the keys up, something like a hand took them, and the kohanim jumped into the fire. Yeshayahu lamented over them, and even God is described as crying out over the destruction.

items.title: When the Megillah is read: the 11th to the 15th
items.summary: The Mishnah says the Megillah is read from the 11th to the 15th of Adar: walled cities on the 15th, towns on the 14th, and villages may read early on the market day, and it lays out every weekday case. The Gemara finds the extra days hinted in the verse's word "in their times," limits them to the 11th and 12th, and rules out later days because "it shall not pass." Rabbi Yochanan says this is Rabbi Akiva's view; after a challenge, the conclusion (backed by Rabbi Yehudah) is that early reading applied only when the Jews lived in their land, and nowadays the Megillah is read only on its own day.

items.title: Yonasan ben Uziel's translation shakes the land
items.summary: Onkelos the convert said the Aramaic translation of the Torah, and Yonasan ben Uziel said the translation of the Prophets, from Chaggai, Zecharyah and Malachi. The land of Israel shook, and a heavenly voice asked who revealed God's secrets; Yonasan answered that he did it for God's honor, so arguments would not multiply in Israel. When he wanted to translate the Writings, a voice said "Enough," because they contain the time of Mashiach. The Gemara explains that the Prophets have hidden passages, which Rav Yosef could not understand without the translation.

items.title: Seventy-two elders translate the Torah for King Ptolemy
items.summary: Rabbi Yehudah says the Sages allowed Greek only for a Sefer Torah, because of King Ptolemy. He put seventy-two elders in seventy-two separate houses and told each to write the Torah of Moshe, and God gave each the same idea, so all made the same changes. The Gemara lists them, such as "God created in the beginning" and writing "the short-legged animal" instead of "hare," so Ptolemy, whose wife was named Arneves, would not think they mocked her.

items.title: The Purim story 1: "And it was in the days of…"
items.summary: Rabbi Levi has a tradition from the Men of the Great Assembly that wherever the Torah says "vayehi" ("and it was"), trouble follows, and gives many examples, starting with Achashverosh and Haman. The Gemara challenges this with happy uses of the word. Rav Ashi concludes: a plain "vayehi" can go either way, but "vayehi bimei" ("and it was in the days of") always means trouble, and there are five such verses.

items.title: The Purim story 2: Achashverosh's feast and Vashti's refusal
items.summary: Achashverosh shows off his riches wearing the kohen gadol's garments, and the Sages argue whether he was clever or foolish. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's students ask why the Jews deserved destruction; he answers that they bowed to an idol only for show, so God threatened them only for show. The Gemara describes the feast's seating, furnishings and wine, and the use of the Temple vessels. At Vashti's feast on the seventh day, which was Shabbos, the king demands she appear unclothed, measure for measure for how she treated Jewish girls; she refuses because of a sudden blemish, and her insulting message makes the king burn with anger.

items.title: The Purim story 3: Esther in the palace
items.summary: The Sages explain Esther's two names and that she was orphaned at birth, and say Mordechai took her as a wife, not just as a daughter. In the palace she counted the days of the week by her seven maids and kept kosher, found favor with everyone, and kept quiet about her people. Her silence is traced to the modesty of Rachel, who gave Leah the secret signs so she would not be shamed, and was rewarded with Shaul and through him Esther. Esther kept asking the Sages about her purity and secretly remained Mordechai's wife.

items.title: The Purim story 4: Bigsan and Teresh, Haman's lottery, and "there is one nation"
items.summary: God made two servants angry at their master to help Mordechai: Bigsan and Teresh plotted in their own language, not knowing Mordechai knew seventy languages. God prepared the cure before the blow, and only then was Haman promoted. Haman's plan grew from Mordechai to the Sages to all the Jews; he rejoiced that the lot fell in Adar, when Moshe died, not knowing Moshe was also born then. Haman slanders the Jews to the king, God makes the Jews' shekels come before Haman's, and the king's handing over of his ring did more to bring the Jews back than all the prophets.

items.title: The Purim story 5: Esther goes to the king, and why she invited Haman
items.summary: When Esther reached the room of idols, the Shechinah left her; she cried "My God, why have You forsaken me?" and wondered if it was because she had called the king a dog, so she called him a lion. Three angels helped her, and the king's scepter was miraculously lengthened. The king offers half his kingdom, but not rebuilding the Temple. The Tannaim and Amoraim give many reasons why Esther invited Haman to her feast, and Eliyahu says she had all of them in mind.

items.title: The Purim story 6: the king's sleepless night and Mordechai on the horse
items.summary: On that night the king could not sleep; he suspects a plot, calls for the records, and they read themselves, with Shimshai erasing and Gavriel rewriting. Haman comes to find Mordechai teaching the laws of the flour offering, and admits their handful of flour beat his ten thousand silver talents. Esther closes the bathhouses and barbershops, so Haman himself must bathe Mordechai and cut his hair, and Mordechai reminds him he was once a village barber. Mordechai climbs onto the horse by stepping on Haman, Haman's daughter dumps a chamber pot on her own father by mistake and falls to her death, Mordechai returns to his sackcloth, and Haman goes home in mourning.

items.title: Watering a field on Chol HaMoed
items.summary: The Mishnah allows watering a thirsty field on Chol HaMoed and in the Shemittah year from a new or an old spring, but not with rainwater or a water-lifting device, and allows public repairs. The Gemara explains that both springs are mentioned to show the kind of spring makes no difference; only a thirsty field may be watered, not a rain-fed one. It asks which Tanna allows work only to prevent a loss and without great effort: Rav Huna's answer, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, is rejected, and Rav Pappa says it is Rabbi Yehudah, who makes no difference between springs.

items.title: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's son and the blessings that sounded like curses
items.summary: Two students take leave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai twice, explaining that a student who sleeps over in town must say goodbye again. He sends his son for their blessing; they wish him to sow and not reap, that his house be ruined and his lodging lived in, that his table be in confusion and that he not see a new year. The son complains that they hurt him, and his father explains each one: many children who live and marry, a long life in this world before the next, a crowded table, and a wife who will not die.

items.summary: The Gemara reads David's last words: he raised up the yoke of repentance, and God told him: I rule over man, and who rules over Me? The tzaddik, for I decree and he cancels it. items.summary: Rav Yehudah bans a Torah scholar with a bad reputation, and on his deathbed is happy he did not flatter him. items.title: Don't mourn more than the Torah asks
items.summary: Rav says that whoever grieves too much over his dead will end up crying over another death. A woman in Rav Huna's neighborhood ignored his warning to stop crying excessively over one of her seven sons, and all of them died, and then she did too. The Gemara sets the limits: three days of crying, seven of eulogy and thirty without ironing or haircuts; beyond that God says, "You are not more merciful to him than I am."

items.title: Life, children and livelihood depend on mazal; how the Sages died
items.summary: Rava says life, children and livelihood depend not on merit but on mazal: Rabbah and Rav Chisda were equally righteous, yet one lived to forty in poverty and loss and the other to ninety-two in wealth and celebration. Rava and Rav Nachman describe after death how painless dying was, though Rav Nachman would not return because of the fear. The Angel of Death waits for Rabbi Elazar, Rav Sheshes and Rav Ashi, can reach Rav Chisda only when his learning stops, and reaches Rabbi Chiya only by disguising himself as a poor man.

items.title: Who must come up to Jerusalem on the festivals
items.summary: The Mishnah says everyone must go up and appear at the Temple on the festivals, except a list of people who are exempt, such as a minor, women, the blind and the lame. The Gemara asks what the word "everyone" comes to add, and tries a person who is half slave and half free, then someone lame on the first day who heals on the second, then someone blind in one eye. It returns to the half-slave and ends with the case of such a person: Beis Shammai argue that he can marry no one, so his master must be forced to free him, and Beis Hillel change their ruling to agree.

items.title: "What was new in the study hall today?" Hakhel and the children
items.summary: Two students visit Rabbi Yehoshua, who asks them what new teaching was said in the study hall that day. They tell him Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah taught that at Hakhel, men come to learn and women to hear, and little children come so that those who bring them earn reward. They pass on more of his teachings, and Rabbi Yehoshua says a generation is not orphaned while Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah lives. The Gemara explains why the students held back at first: once, when Rabbi Eliezer heard that the Sages had voted on a law he knew as a tradition from Sinai, his visitor Rabbi Yossi lost his sight, and later Rabbi Eliezer prayed and it came back.

items.title: The rabbis who wept at verses about judgment
items.summary: One after another, Rav Huna, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi cry when they reach certain verses: a servant whom his master longs to see may still be pushed away, if Shmuel the prophet feared judgment so should we, and "all this, and only perhaps?" Rav Yosef cries at the verse about people swept away without justice. The Gemara answers with a story told to Rav Bibi bar Abaye: the Angel of Death's messenger brought the wrong Miriam, and the angel kept her anyway. Her lost years, he explains, are added to a Torah scholar who lets wrongs done to him pass.

items.title: Reviewing 100 times versus 101
items.summary: Bar Hei Hei asks Hillel why a verse in Malachi seems to say the same thing twice, contrasting "one who serves God" with "one who did not serve Him". Hillel answers that both are completely righteous, but someone who reviews his learning 100 times is not like someone who reviews it 101 times. When Bar Hei Hei asks if one extra time really earns that name, Hillel points to the donkey drivers' market: ten parsahs cost one zuz, but eleven cost two.

items.title: The fifteen women
items.summary: The first Mishnah in Yevamot lists fifteen close relatives of a man (like his daughter or his wife's sister) who, if married to his brother who dies childless, are exempt from yibum and chalitzah with him, and free their co-wives too, even down a long chain. It explains how this works and when it does not, for example if the relative died or was divorced before the brother died. The Gemara then asks why the list starts with his daughter and not his wife's sister, tries an order by severity of punishment and rejects it, and concludes that the list follows closeness of relation, with a few cases grouped together for convenience.

items.title: Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas and his younger brother
items.summary: The Sages hear that a ruling like Beis Shammai was given in the name of the elderly Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, and Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and Rabbi Akiva go to visit him. He welcomes each warmly and tells them the law follows Beis Hillel. When they say the other ruling was quoted in his name, he explains it came from his younger brother Yonasan, a student of Shammai, and warns them that Yonasan has 300 arguments ready. Leaving, they meet Yonasan, who challenges Rabbi Akiva and tells him he is famous but has not yet reached the level of cattle herders, and Rabbi Akiva humbly answers: not even of shepherds.

items.title: How a convert is accepted
items.summary: A Baraisa teaches that when someone comes to convert, the court first asks him why, since the Jewish people suffer, and if he says he knows this and is not even worthy, they accept him right away. They teach him some easy and some serious mitzvos, warn him of punishments, tell him of the reward, and do not overload him; then he is circumcised and, once healed, immerses, after which he is a full Jew. The Gemara explains each step: the warnings are so that anyone who will drop out drops out now, Naomi's words to Ruth are the model, and the circumcision is done at once because a mitzvah is not delayed. It ends by teaching that even if he later turns away, his marriage to a Jewish woman is valid.

items.title: Rabban Gamliel's shipwreck: Rabbi Akiva saved by a plank
items.summary: Rabban Gamliel tells how he saw a ship break apart and grieved for Rabbi Akiva, who was on it, but when he reached land Rabbi Akiva came and discussed halacha with him. Rabbi Akiva explained that a plank came his way and he bowed his head to every wave, and the Sages learned from this to bow your head when wicked people come against you. Rabbi Akiva tells a matching story about Rabbi Meir, whom one wave passed to the next until he was thrown onto dry land. Both say the story showed how wise the Sages were not to let a wife remarry when her husband was lost in water with no visible end.

items.title: Why a wedding is on a Wednesday
items.summary: The Mishnah says a first-time bride marries on Wednesday and a widow on Thursday, because the courts sit on Mondays and Thursdays, so a husband with a complaint about her virginity can go to court the next morning. The Gemara first tries a version of Shmuel's teaching that ties the rule to when the groom must start feeding the bride, rejects it, and gives the correct version: the reason is the court. Why not marry on Sunday? Because the Sages cared for Jewish women and wanted the groom to spend three days preparing the wedding feast. So if the set date falls on Sunday, or either of them is sick, he does not yet have to provide her food.

The hint is Yaakov's promise, "I will surely give a tenth": two tenths make a fifth.

items.title: Nakdimon ben Gurion's daughter gathers barley
items.summary: Leaving Jerusalem, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai sees a young woman picking barley out of animal dung, and she asks him for help: she is the daughter of the once-rich Nakdimon ben Gurion. He remembers signing her kesubah, worth a million gold dinars, and cries that when Israel does not do God's will they are handed over even to the animals of a lowly nation. The Gemara asks whether Nakdimon gave no charity, and answers that he gave for his own honor, or not as much as he should have. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok adds that he saw her gathering barley between horses' hooves in Akko.

items.title: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi takes the knife of the Angel of Death
items.summary: While other rabbis kept far from people with a contagious disease, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sat with them and learned Torah, trusting it to protect him. When he was about to die, he asked the Angel of Death to show him his place in Gan Eden and to lend him his knife, then jumped over to the other side and swore he would not come back. God ruled that since he had never had an oath undone, he could stay; he had to return the knife, and Eliyahu announced, "Make room for the son of Levi!" Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai asked him whether a rainbow had been seen in his lifetime, and the Gemara says he answered yes only so as not to take credit for himself.

items.title: Rabbi's maid prays and drops the jar
items.summary: On the day Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) died, the Sages fasted and prayed for him. His maid first prayed that the people below would win over the angels above, but when she saw how he suffered, she prayed the opposite, and she threw a jar from the roof so the Sages would stop praying for a moment, and he died. Bar Kappara broke the news in a parable about the holy ark being captured, letting the Sages say the words themselves. Rabbi's last prayer was that his rest be peaceful, and a heavenly voice answered with a verse, which the Gemara explains: the righteous come out to greet a new righteous person.

items.title: The judges who stepped aside over a tiny favor
items.summary: A Baraisa teaches that even a bribe of words is forbidden. Shmuel, Ameimar and Mar Ukva each refuse to judge a man's case after he did them a small favor: helping them off a ferry, removing a feather from their head, covering spit. Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha each turn down a gift from someone with a case and hand it to other judges, yet catch themselves thinking of arguments for that person. Each says: if I feel this way without taking anything, how much more those who take bribes!

items.title: Substitute words that make a vow
items.summary: The first Mishnah in Nedarim says that substitute words for vows, for dedications, for oaths and for nazirite vows all count like the real thing, and that partial phrases like "I am avowed from you" or "what I eat of yours" also forbid. The Gemara asks why this Mishnah lists all four kinds, why it orders them as it does, and why it opens with substitute words but explains the partial phrases first. It concludes that some words are missing from the Mishnah: partial phrases also count as vows. It finds their source in the Torah's doubled wording about the nazir, extended to ordinary vows by comparing the two.

items.title: Rabbi Akiva's wife: the straw bed and Eliyahu
items.summary: Kalba Savua's daughter married Rabbi Akiva against her father's wishes, and he vowed she would get nothing from him. They were so poor they slept on straw, and Rabbi Akiva promised her a golden crown of Jerusalem if he could; Eliyahu came disguised as a man begging for straw, so they saw others had even less. She sent him to learn for twelve years, and when he overheard her say she would happily let him stay twelve more, he went back. He returned with 24,000 pairs of students, told them that all his Torah and theirs was hers, and her father came and had his vow undone.

items.title: Rabbi Tarfon's regret: learning Torah for its own sake
items.summary: A farmer found Rabbi Tarfon eating leftover fruit after the harvest, put him in a sack to throw him in the river, and fled when Rabbi Tarfon cried that the man was killing Tarfon. All his life Rabbi Tarfon was pained that he had used the crown of Torah to save himself, since he was rich and could have paid instead. A Baraisa then teaches not to learn Torah in order to be called wise or Rabbi, but out of love, and the honor will come. Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok adds: do not make Torah a crown to make yourself great or an axe to dig with.

items.title: The Babylonian husband and the two lamps
items.summary: A man from Babylonia moved to the Land of Israel and married a local woman who kept taking his Babylonian words literally: asked for two lentils, she cooked exactly two. When he asked for two melons (in his dialect), she brought two lamps, and he told her to break them on the head of the "bava" (the gate). She broke them on the head of the sage Bava ben Buta, who was judging at the gate. When she explained her husband had told her to, he blessed her: since she did her husband's will, may she have two sons like Bava ben Buta.

items.title: Why the sons of scholars don't always become scholars
items.summary: A message from the Land of Israel warns: take care with the sons of the poor, because Torah will come from them. The Gemara asks why Torah scholars' sons often do not become scholars, and the rabbis give answers: so people won't think Torah is inherited, because the scholars act superior or call people donkeys, or, says Ravina, because they do not say a blessing on Torah before learning. Rav explains that this is why the land was destroyed, a question no sage or prophet could answer until God said: because they left My Torah.

items.title: The words that make someone a nazir
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Nazir lists the words that make a person a nazir: the word itself, look-alike words, and short phrases like "I will be" or "I will be beautiful". The Gemara asks why Nazir is placed among the tractates about marriage, and why the Mishnah explains its items in the order it does. Then it asks how "I will be" can mean a nazir, when he might have meant "I will be fasting". Shmuel answers that a nazir was passing in front of him, and the Gemara concludes that his words count as long as he meant nazirus.

items.title: Shimon HaTzaddik and the handsome shepherd who became a nazir
items.summary: Shimon HaTzaddik said he never ate the guilt offering of a nazir who became impure, except once. A young man came to him from the South, with beautiful eyes and his hair in curls. He explained that he was a shepherd, saw his reflection in a spring, and felt his evil inclination rise up in pride, so he swore to cut his hair for the sake of Heaven. Shimon HaTzaddik kissed him on the head and said: may there be more nazirim like you in Israel.

items.title: Queen Helene's years as a nazir
items.summary: The Mishnah: someone who finished a long nazirus outside the Land of Israel and then came there must start again, according to Beis Hillel. Queen Helene vowed to be a nazir for seven years if her son came home safely from war. After seven years she came to the Land, Beis Hillel ruled she must keep seven more, and at the end of those she became impure, so she was a nazir for twenty-one years. Rabbi Yehudah says it was only fourteen, and the Gemara proves that in his telling she never became impure.

items.title: A sin for the sake of Heaven: Tamar, Yael and Ruth
items.summary: Ulla compares Tamar and Zimri: both sinned, but kings and prophets came from Tamar, while many thousands of Jews fell because of Zimri. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak teaches that a sin for the sake of Heaven is like a mitzvah done for the wrong reasons, and proves it from Yael, who is praised like the Matriarchs. Then the Gemara shows the value of doing mitzvos even for the wrong reasons: as a reward for the offerings the wicked Balak brought, Ruth came from him.

end.words: רוּת, בַּת בְּנוֹ שֶׁל עֶגְלוֹן מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב הָיְתָה.

items.title: Torah scholars increase peace in the world: the end of Nazir
items.summary: The last Mishnah of Nazir proves that Shmuel the prophet was a nazir, and Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Nehorai argue about it. The Gemara asks whether it is greater to say a blessing or to answer amen. It ends Nazir with Rabbi Elazar's teaching in the name of Rabbi Chanina: Torah scholars increase peace in the world.

items.title: Warning and seclusion: how the Sotah process starts
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Sotah: a husband warns his wife in front of two witnesses not to be alone with a certain man. Just talking to him changes nothing, but if she then goes into a hidden place with him long enough to sin, she becomes forbidden to her husband. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua argue about how many witnesses each step needs. Along the way the Gemara teaches that finding a match is as hard as splitting the sea, and it concludes that one witness is believed that she actually sinned.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends once it is settled that one witness is believed about the sin itself. The Gemara's sources for how many witnesses the warning and the seclusion need continue on 2b (steps 10 to 22).

items.title: Tamar would rather be burned than shame Yehudah
items.summary: When Tamar was taken out to be burned, she did not name Yehudah. She only sent him his belongings, saying she was pregnant by the man they belonged to. From this the Gemara teaches that it is better to be thrown into a fiery furnace than to shame someone in public. Yehudah admitted, 'She is more righteous than I,' and because he sanctified Hashem's name in public, a heavenly voice promised that three of his descendants, Chananiah, Mishael and Azariah, would be saved from fire.

items.title: The righteous women in Egypt
items.summary: Rav Avira taught that Israel was redeemed from Egypt in the merit of the righteous women of that generation. When they drew water, Hashem put small fish in their jugs, and they cooked and brought food to their husbands in the fields and cared for them. They gave birth in the fields, Hashem sent someone to care for the babies, and when the Egyptians came to kill them the ground swallowed them up. The babies grew up, came home in flocks, and at the sea they were the first to recognize Hashem and say, 'This is my God.'

items.title: Esav at the Cave of Machpelah; Moshe finds Yosef's bones
items.summary: At Yaakov's funeral, kings came and hung their crowns on his coffin. At the Cave of Machpelah, Esav blocked the burial and claimed the last grave. The brothers said he had sold it, and sent Naftali running to Egypt for the document, but Chushim son of Dan, who could not hear well, struck Esav down. Later, when Israel left Egypt, Moshe learned from Serach bas Asher where Yosef was buried, called to him, and the coffin rose up, and Yosef's coffin traveled in the desert beside the Ark.

end.words: קִיֵּים זֶה כׇּל מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בָּזֶה.

items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. The Gemara gives two versions of where Yosef was buried, the Nile (step 25) and the royal tombs (steps 28 to 29); the summary does not choose between them.

items.title: Yosef sees his father's face and does not sin
items.summary: Rabbi Shimon Chasida teaches that Yosef sanctified Hashem's name in private, so a letter of Hashem's name was added to his own. The Gemara explains: on the day everyone went to their idol festival, Potiphar's wife stayed home and grabbed Yosef by his garment. At that moment the image of his father appeared to him in the window and warned him that he would lose his place among his brothers on the stones of the Ephod. Yosef overcame his desire, and so his name was engraved on the Ephod.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. items.title: Why the messenger must say "it was written and signed before me"
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Gittin: a messenger who brings a get from overseas must say, 'It was written in front of me and signed in front of me.' The Tannaim argue about which places count as 'overseas', and inside the Land of Israel no statement is needed. The Gemara gives two reasons: Rabbah says people there do not know that a get must be written for this woman, and Rava says no witnesses are around to confirm the signatures. It then lists the cases where the two reasons give different rulings.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends where the practical differences between Rabbah and Rava are listed. The Gemara goes on (2b step 7 to 3a) to ask why one messenger is enough, and why each Amora rejects the other's reason.

items.title: Hillel's prozbul
items.summary: Hillel saw that people stopped lending money before the Shemitah year, which cancels debts, so he made the prozbul: the lender hands his debts over to the court, so they can be collected after Shemitah. The Gemara asks how Hillel could undo a Torah law. Abaye answers that nowadays Shemitah cancels debts only by rabbinic law, and Rava adds that a court can declare property ownerless. Then Shmuel says he would cancel the prozbul if he could, and Rav Nachman says he would strengthen it.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The Mishnah line ('Hillel made the prozbul') is back on 34b, inside a long list of enactments, so the range starts where the Gemara takes it up.

items.title: Then: Titus and the gnat
items.summary: After the meeting with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakai, Vespasian sent Titus, who defiled the Holy of Holies, slashed the curtain, and loaded the Temple’s vessels onto a ship. When a storm rose at sea, he mocked Hashem and dared Him to fight on dry land, and a gnat entered his brain and tormented him for seven years until he died. Onkelos, Titus’s nephew, who wanted to convert, raised him from the dead and asked who is most important in that world. Titus said: Israel, but advised him to fight them instead, and told him his own punishment: his ashes are gathered, judged and burned again every day.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Follow-on to git55b-kamtza, which ends at 56b step 14; this starts on the next step. It ends with Titus’s punishment (57a step 1), before Onkelos raises two more figures (57a steps 2 to 7, a delicate passage); so Rabbi Elazar’s closing line about the power of shame (57a step 8) is left out.

items.title: The captive children and the mother with seven sons
items.summary: Four hundred boys and girls were taken captive for shame, and they drowned themselves in the sea rather than be abused. The Gemara says the verse 'For Your sake we are killed all day long' is about them, and Rav Yehudah says it is about the woman and her seven sons. Each son was ordered to worship an idol, answered with a verse from the Torah, and was killed. The seventh would not even bend down to pick up the emperor's ring. His mother kissed him and told him to tell Avraham: you bound one altar, I bound seven. Then she died, and a heavenly voice said, 'The mother of the children is joyful.'
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Starts with the captive children (step 15) because the mother's story is given as Rav Yehudah's other reading of the same verse. items.title: Rabbi Yehoshua ransoms a boy in Rome: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
items.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah went to Rome and heard about a beautiful child in prison. He stood at the prison door and quoted half a verse: 'Who gave Yaakov over to be plundered?' The child answered with the rest of the verse: 'Was it not Hashem, against Whom we sinned?' Rabbi Yehoshua swore not to leave until he ransomed him, whatever the price. He did, and within a few days the boy was ruling on halachah in Israel: he was Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The next story (steps 20 to 22), about Rabbi Yishmael's captive son and daughter, is a separate teaching of Rav and is left out.

items.title: Shlomo, Ashmedai and the shamir
items.summary: Shlomo needed the shamir to cut the Temple's stones without iron. Demons told him only Ashmedai, their king, would know where it was. Benayahu son of Yehoyada filled Ashmedai's well with wine, and when Ashmedai drank and fell asleep, he chained him with Hashem's Name and brought him back. On the way Ashmedai did strange things, cried at a wedding, laughed at a man ordering shoes, and later explained each one. He told Shlomo who held the shamir, Shlomo's men tricked a wild rooster into bringing it, and Shlomo kept Ashmedai until the Temple was built.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: A self-contained first part. The story goes on (68b steps 21 to 33): Ashmedai tricks Shlomo, throws him far away, and Shlomo wanders as a beggar until he returns. That could be a 'Then:' follow-on starting at 68b step 21.

items.title: Rav Acha bar Yaakov and the seven-headed demon; learning or marrying first
items.summary: If a father and son both need to learn Torah, the father comes first, unless the son is quick and remembers what he learns. Rav Acha bar Yaakov sent his son to Abaye, saw he came back not sharp, and went to learn himself. Abaye had no one host him, so he slept in the study hall where a demon harmed people, and it looked to him like a seven-headed snake, and each time he bowed one head fell off. Then the Gemara asks whether to learn Torah first or marry first. Shmuel says marry first, Rabbi Yochanan asks how anyone can learn with a millstone around his neck, and the Gemara says each ruling fits a different place.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The Gemara only says 'this one is for us, and that one is for them' (step 29). Which ruling is for Bavel and which for the Land of Israel is Rashi's explanation, so the summary does not say.

items.title: "I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its antidote"
items.summary: Torah is compared to a medicine of life: like a father who bandages his son's wound and tells him that as long as the bandage stays on he can eat and drink freely. So Hashem told Israel: I created the evil inclination and I created Torah as its cure, and if you are busy with Torah it will not rule you. The evil inclination is so bad that even its Creator calls it evil, it renews itself every day, and only Hashem's help lets a person overcome it. The school of Rabbi Yishmael says: if it meets you, drag it to the study hall; if it is stone it melts, and if it is iron it shatters.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: Is the reward for mitzvos in this world?
items.summary: The Mishnah says that whoever does one mitzvah is treated well and lives long. The Gemara asks how that fits a teaching that the righteous often suffer, and Rava answers that this follows Rabbi Yaakov, who says there is no reward for mitzvos in this world. His proof: a boy climbed up at his father's word and sent away the mother bird, both mitzvos promised long life, and he fell and died, so the promise must be about the World to Come. Rav Yosef says that if Acher had read the verse like Rabbi Yaakov, his grandson, he would not have sinned, and the Gemara gives two versions of what Acher saw.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends after the Acher story. The next question (whether someone who just avoids sin is rewarded) and the story of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi start at step 28 and run onto 40a.

items.title: King Yannai and the tzitz
items.summary: King Yannai returned from a victory and celebrated with all the Sages. A wicked man, Elazar ben Po'irah, told him the Pharisees were secretly against him, and told him to test them by wearing the tzitz, the High Priest's gold plate. An elder, Yehudah ben Gedidiah, told the king to leave the priesthood to Aharon's descendants, since people said his mother had been a captive, but it was checked and not proven. On Elazar's advice the king had the Sages killed, and the world was desolate until Shimon ben Shatach restored the Torah.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The story is brought as Abaye's proof that one witness is believed; steps 17 to 20 go back to that argument and are left out.

items.title: False witnesses: when they don't get what they plotted
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Makkos: if witnesses falsely say a kohen is the son of a divorced woman, or that someone must go into exile, and are proven to be plotting witnesses, they do not get that same punishment; they get forty lashes instead. The Gemara explains that this continues the end of Sanhedrin, where plotting witnesses usually get what they plotted. It learns from 'to him', not to his children, that they cannot be made unfit kohanim, and from 'he shall flee' that they are not exiled. Finally Ulla finds the verse that gives them lashes.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The proposed title said they 'get what they plotted', but this Mishnah is about the exceptions, so the title was changed.

items.title: The cities of refuge, and a student's exile brings his teacher
items.summary: The cities of refuge had to be medium-sized towns with water, markets and people, and nothing may be done there that would bring the avenger of blood around. Since the verse says the killer flees there 'and lives', everything he needs to live is provided, so when a student is exiled, his teacher goes with him, and when a teacher is exiled, his yeshivah goes with him. The Gemara says Torah itself protects, but only while one is learning, and tells how the Angel of Death could not come near Rav Chisda until he stopped learning for a moment.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Step 20 offers a second answer: Torah protects from the Angel of Death, and the Rav Chisda story (step 21) illustrates it.

items.title: The kohen gadol's mother feeds the exiled killers
items.summary: The Mishnah says the death of the kohen gadol lets the accidental killer go home, so the mothers of the kohanim would bring the exiles food and clothing, so they would not pray for their sons to die. The Gemara asks why a prayer against an innocent kohen gadol would work. An elder answers in Rava's name that the kohen gadol should have prayed for his generation and did not. The Gemara compares the man eaten by a lion near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, after which Eliyahu did not speak to him for three days.

end.words: וְלָא אִישְׁתַּעִי אֵלִיָּהוּ בַּהֲדֵיהּ תְּלָתָא יוֹמֵי.

items.title: Hazards left in the public street
items.summary: The Mishnah rules that someone who pours water into the street, hides thorns or glass, or lets his thorn fence or wall fall into the public way must pay for any damage. The Gemara limits each case: Rav says the water case covers only soiled clothes, and Rabbi Yochanan says hidden thorns make him liable only if they stick out into the street. It ends with the early pious people, who buried their thorns and glass deep in their own fields, and Rav Yehudah's advice: whoever wants to be pious should keep the laws of damages.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends with the 'one who wants to be pious' lines (steps 19 to 22), which close the thorns discussion naturally; the next step opens a new Mishnah.

items.title: Nechunya the well-digger's daughter
items.summary: Nechunya dug wells and pits and handed them over to the public, and the Sages praised him for keeping this law. When his daughter fell into a deep pit, Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa said 'All is well' for two hours and in the third said 'She has come up'; she said an old man leading a ram had pulled her out. Rabbi Chanina explained he was no prophet: the children of a righteous man could not stumble through the very thing he worked for. Rabbi Acha adds that even so, Nechunya's son died of thirst, because God judges those close to Him to a hair's breadth.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Starts with the short legal teaching about handing a pit to the public, which introduces Nechunya; ends with Rabbi Chanina's line 'whoever says God lets things go', which rounds off the theme.

items.title: David's question about the barley stacks
items.summary: David longed for water from the well of Beis Lechem, and three warriors broke through the Philistine camp to bring it. The Gemara says this was really a halachic question: either about hidden things burned in a fire, or whether one may save himself by destroying another person's property (Jewish barley stacks where Philistines were hiding, or barley to be swapped for Philistine lentils). The answer sent back: an ordinary person may not, but a king may break through to make a path. The Gemara then reads 'he would not drink it' and 'he poured it out to God' as David refusing to quote the law in the names of men who had risked their lives.

items.title: Why a thief pays double but a robber doesn't
items.summary: Rabbi Elazar rules that a thief seen hiding in the woods still pays the four-or-five-times penalty, because he hid from people. The Gemara asks what a robber is, and Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Yochanan give examples of open, armed taking. Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's students ask why the Torah is stricter with the thief, and he answers that the thief fears people more than God, acting as if God's eye does not see. It ends with two teachings on why an ox pays five and a sheep four: the value of work, and the dignity of the thief who had to carry the sheep.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. items.title: Rav Kahana and Rabbi Yochanan's eyebrows
items.summary: A man insists on informing on his fellow's straw to the authorities, and Rav Kahana kills him; Rav sends him to Eretz Yisrael and tells him not to challenge Rabbi Yochanan for seven years. Reish Lakish calls him a lion, but at first he sits silent and is moved back seven rows; then he starts challenging until Rabbi Yochanan sits on the floor without his cushions. The old Rabbi Yochanan has his drooping eyebrows lifted, sees Rav Kahana's split lip, thinks he is laughing at him, and Rav Kahana dies. Rabbi Yochanan goes to the cave, the serpent lets the student in to the teacher, he prays and brings Rav Kahana back to life, and Rav Kahana answers all his questions.

items.title: Your father's lost object or your teacher's: which first?
items.summary: The Mishnah rules that your own lost object comes before your father's or teacher's, and your teacher's comes before your father's, because your father brought you into this world and your teacher brings you to the World to Come, unless your father is himself a sage. The Gemara learns 'your own comes first' from a verse but warns that someone who always insists on it will end up poor. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Yosi argue about who counts as 'his teacher', with stories of Rava and Shmuel and the falling-out of Rav Chisda and Rav Huna. It concludes that the Mishnah's 'teacher who taught him wisdom' means the one who taught him most of his wisdom.

items.title: Hurting with words, and shaming someone in public
items.summary: The Mishnah teaches that just as one may not cheat in money, one may not hurt with words: do not remind a penitent of his past or ask a seller a price when you do not mean to buy. The Gemara adds that hurting with words is worse than cheating with money, because it hurts the person himself and cannot be paid back. Shaming someone in public is like spilling blood, and is one of three sins whose doers go down to Gehinnom and do not come up. It ends with the teaching that it is better to throw yourself into a fiery furnace than shame someone publicly, learned from Tamar.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends with Tamar (59a step 7); 59a continues with more sayings about hurtful words and one's wife before the oven of Akhnai at step 23, so there is no overlap.

items.title: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon catches thieves for the government
items.summary: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon teaches a Roman officer how to spot thieves, and the king then appoints Rabbi Elazar himself to catch them. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah rebukes him as 'vinegar son of wine' for handing Jews over to death. When a laundryman insults him the same way, Rabbi Elazar has him arrested, regrets it, cannot save him and weeps at the gallows, until he hears the man was truly wicked. Still unsettled, he undergoes surgery, and his removed fat does not rot in the summer sun, which he takes as proof that he acted rightly.
