items.title: Rabbah bar Nachmani is called to the heavenly yeshiva
items.summary: Rabbah bar Nachmani is slandered to the king for keeping thousands of Jews from the head tax, and flees from town to town. He escapes custody and learns in a swamp, while the heavenly yeshiva disputes a question about leprous marks and decides that Rabbah must settle it. The Angel of Death cannot take him while he learns, until a rustle in the reeds stops him; he dies saying 'pure, pure', and a heavenly voice praises him. A note from heaven tells the Rabbis, birds shade his body, and a storm on the day he died calms only when an Arab merchant prays.

items.title: Avraham's guests and the three calves
items.summary: The Gemara reads 'a calf, tender and good' as three calves, so that Avraham could serve his three guests three tongues with mustard. It teaches that whatever Avraham did for the angels himself, God did for his children Himself, and what he did through a messenger, God did through a messenger. It then explains that the visit came on the third day after Avraham's circumcision, when God brought out the sun so he would not be bothered by guests, yet Avraham went out looking for them. The three men were the angels Michael, Gavriel and Refael, each with his own task.

items.title: Rav in the cemetery: what is 'all sickness'?
items.summary: On the verse 'God will remove from you all sickness', Rav says it means the evil eye: he visited a cemetery and declared that ninety-nine had died of the evil eye and one naturally. Shmuel says it is the wind, Rabbi Chanina says the cold, and others say bodily waste or gall. The Gemara says a morning meal of bread with salt and a jug of water protects against all of them, and lists the benefits of eating in the morning, learned from verses.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: The cemetery story itself is one line ('he did what he did'); the passage is built as the five views of 'all sickness' plus the morning meal that closes the topic.

items.title: Herod and Bava ben Buta
items.summary: The Gemara asks how Bava ben Buta could advise Herod to tear down the Temple before rebuilding it. Herod, a slave of the Hasmoneans, killed his masters and the Sages, sparing only Bava ben Buta, whom he blinded. Disguised, Herod tries to get him to curse the king, but Bava ben Buta refuses; Herod reveals himself and asks how to repent, and is told to rebuild the Temple, sending a slow messenger to Rome so the work would be done before an answer came. The Gemara ends with praise of Herod's marble building, which the Sages told him not to cover with gold.

start.words: וּבָבָא בֶּן בּוּטָא, הֵיכִי אַסְּבֵיהּ לֵיהּ עֵצָה

items.title: Rabbi opens his storehouses
items.summary: In a drought Rabbi opened his storehouses only to those who had learned Torah. Yonasan ben Amram pushed in and asked to be fed 'like a dog and a raven', and Rabbi fed him but then regretted giving bread to an ignorant man. His son suggested it was his humble student Yonasan, who never wanted benefit from his Torah; it was so, and Rabbi let everyone in. The Gemara links this to Rabbi's view that trouble comes because of the unlearned, shown by a crown tax in Tiberias that disappeared once everyone but the Rabbis fled.

items.title: Charity that saves from death, and "I saw an upside-down world"
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan asks why two verses say 'charity saves from death', and answers that one saves from an unusual death and one from Gehinnom; the first is charity given so that the giver and receiver do not know each other, through a trustworthy charity fund. Rabbi Abahu brings Shlomo's answers on the power of charity and on who earns the World to Come. Then Yosef son of Rabbi Yehoshua faints and sees an upside-down world, where the important are low and the lowly high, and Torah scholars and martyrs are honored.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Starts after the existing Turnus Rufus Classic (10a steps 3 to 9) with no overlap. Joins two adjacent pieces: the best way to give charity (to 10b step 6) and the upside-down world (10b steps 12 to 21), with short sayings on charity in between.

items.title: Binyamin HaTzaddik and King Monbaz give away their treasures
items.summary: Binyamin HaTzaddik, in charge of the charity fund, fed a starving woman and her seven sons from his own money when the fund was empty; when he later lay dying, the angels pleaded for him and twenty-two years were added to his life. King Monbaz gave away his and his fathers' treasures in years of drought, and when his family protested he answered that his fathers stored treasures below and he stored them above, money that bears fruit, treasures of souls, kept for himself and for the World to Come.

items.title: The order of the books of Tanach, and who wrote each one
items.summary: A teaching gives the order of the Prophets and the Writings, and the Gemara explains surprises: Yeshayahu is placed after Yirmiyahu and Yechezkel so that destruction sits next to destruction and comfort next to comfort, and the Writings do not open with Iyov's suffering. It then lists who wrote each book: Moshe, Yehoshua, Shmuel, David with ten elders, Yirmiyahu, Chizkiyahu's group, the Men of the Great Assembly and Ezra. The Gemara asks how a book could record its own author's death, and answers that someone else finished it, including the debate over who wrote the last eight verses of the Torah.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Long (about 38 steps). Ends after the discussion of David's ten elders; 15a step 25 onward turns to when Iyov lived.

items.title: Then: Rabbah bar Bar Chana in the desert: Korach and Mount Sinai
items.summary: Rabbah bar Bar Chana sees geese so fat that oil flows from them, and an Arab guide who finds his way by smelling the dust. The guide shows him the giant 'dead of the wilderness'; he cuts a corner of one's tzitzis and cannot move until he returns it, and the Sages later scold him. At Mount Sinai he hears a heavenly voice regretting an oath, and at the place where Korach's group was swallowed he hears them saying 'Moshe and his Torah are true, and they are liars.' Finally he sees where earth and sky meet, and his basket is carried away by the turning sky.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Follow-on to the existing 'Rabbah bar Bar Chana's sea stories' Classic, which ends at 73b step 12; this starts at step 13.

items.title: "Two that are four": the opening of Shevuot
items.summary: The Mishnah opens with four sets of 'two that are really four': oaths, awareness of impurity, carrying out on Shabbos, and shades of leprous marks. It then explains which offering atones for someone who entered the Temple or ate sacred food while impure, depending on whether he knew at the start, at the end, both or neither, with Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir disagreeing about the different goat offerings. The Gemara explains why Shevuot follows Makkos, why the Mishnah lists all four sets, and what the two and the four are in each set.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Long (about 39 steps) because the opening Mishnah itself runs from 2a to 2b step 16. Ends where the Gemara finishes explaining the four sets; the next step asks whose view the Mishnah follows.

items.title: "Remember" and "keep" were said in one word
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan says that an oath about the future is called a 'false' oath and one about the past an oath 'in vain', each with its own prohibition. When a teaching says that 'in vain' and 'false' are one, the Gemara explains that they were said in a single utterance, just as 'Remember' and 'Keep' the Shabbos were said in one word, something no human mouth can say or ear can hear. From 'Remember' and 'Keep' Rav Ada bar Ahavah learns that women must make Kiddush. The Gemara concludes that the link teaches lashes for a false oath just as for an oath in vain, or a sacrifice for both, following Rabbi Akiva.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: 'Remember and keep' is one proof inside a sugya about two kinds of oaths; the passage covers that sugya from Rabbi Yochanan's statement to its two answers.

items.title: Keep far from a lie: the judge, the student and the creditor
items.summary: A teaching applies 'Keep far from a false matter' to many cases. A judge must not defend his own mistaken ruling, sit with a robber colleague, or decide a case he knows is crooked and blame the witnesses. A student must speak up when he sees his teacher erring, and must not even stand silently beside his teacher's single witness. A creditor must not inflate his claim to force an oath, both sides must be dressed alike in court, and a judge must not hear one side before the other arrives.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: The whole world trembled at "do not take God's name in vain"
items.summary: Before a court oath, the judges warn the person: the whole world shook when God said at Sinai 'Do not take God's name in vain.' Unlike other sins, this one is 'not cleared', is punished on the sinner's family and the whole world, and is punished at once, consuming the house of the false swearer. If he refuses to swear he is sent away; if he agrees, the onlookers say 'Move away from the tents of these wicked men.' He is told the oath follows the court's meaning and God's, just as Moshe told Israel when he made them swear.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Starts on 38b (the end of the amud) where the teaching opens; the proposed 39a is where it continues.

items.title: Is a judge allowed to make a compromise?
items.summary: A teaching says that a compromise, like a court case, needs three judges, and once the verdict is given it is too late for one. Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yose HaGelili says compromise is forbidden and the judge must 'let the law pierce the mountain', while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says it is a mitzvah, since the only 'judgment of peace' is a compromise. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya allows a judge to suggest compromise only until he knows which way the case leans. Rav rules like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, and the Gemara explains that the 'mitzvah' is to ask the two sides: do you want strict law, or a compromise?

end.words: אִי אַתָּה רַשַּׁאי לוֹמַר לָהֶן ״צְאוּ וּבִצְעוּ״.

items.title: Eldad and Medad
items.summary: When God told Moshe to gather seventy elders, two men, Eldad and Medad, stayed in the camp. One view says Moshe held a lottery with seventy-two slips, two of them blank, so that no tribe would feel cheated (and the Gemara tells of a similar lottery for the firstborns). Rabbi Shimon says they stayed behind out of humility, and God rewarded them with prophecy that never stopped. The Gemara gives three views of what they prophesied (Moshe will die and Yehoshua will bring Israel into the land; the quail; Gog and Magog), and explains Yehoshua's request to 'restrain them' as: give them the community's needs to handle, and they will stop on their own.

items.title: King Yannai is put on trial before Shimon ben Shetach
items.summary: Rav Yosef says the Mishnah's rule that a king is not judged applies only to the kings of Israel, not to kings from David's family. Why not judge the kings of Israel? Because King Yannai's slave killed a man, and Shimon ben Shetach had the king himself summoned to stand at the trial. Yannai refused to stand unless the other judges agreed, and when Shimon ben Shetach turned to them, they all looked down at the ground. Shimon ben Shetach cursed them, the angel Gavriel struck them and they died, and from then on it was ruled that a king does not judge and is not judged.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: "My creations are drowning and you sing?"
items.summary: A verse says there was song in the camp when the wicked King Achav died. The Gemara asks: does God rejoice when the wicked fall? Rabbi Yonasan points out that one praise in Tanach leaves out 'for He is good', and that when the Egyptians drowned at the sea, God stopped the angels from singing: 'My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you sing before Me?' Rabbi Yose bar Chanina answers that God Himself does not rejoice, but He lets others rejoice.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: Antoninus and Rabbi: the blind man and the lame man
items.summary: Antoninus tells Rabbi that body and soul can each escape judgment: the body blames the soul, which flew off like a bird, and the soul blames the body, which lies in the grave like a stone. Rabbi answers with a parable: a king set a lame man and a blind man to guard his orchard of fine early figs, and the lame man rode on the blind man's shoulders so they could take the figs and eat them. Each one claimed he could not have done it, so the owner put the lame man back on the blind man and judged them together. So too, God puts the soul back into the body and judges them as one.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: Chizkiyahu could have been the Mashiach
items.summary: In a verse in Yeshayahu, a mem in the middle of a word is written in its closed, final form. Bar Kappara explains: God wanted to make King Chizkiyahu the Mashiach and Sancheiriv into Gog and Magog, but the attribute of justice objected that Chizkiyahu never sang a song of praise after all the miracles done for him, so the mem was closed. The earth offered to sing in his place and the angel over the world pleaded for him, but a heavenly voice answered: 'My secret is Mine.' When the prophet cried 'Until when?', the answer was: until traitors and robbers come.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: Rabbi Akiva laughs at Rabbi Eliezer's sickbed
items.summary: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students cried, but Rabbi Akiva laughed: as long as everything his teacher owned prospered, he had feared Rabbi Eliezer was receiving all his reward in this world, and now he was glad; when Rabbi Eliezer asked if he had left out anything in the Torah, Rabbi Akiva answered that no righteous person never sins. In a second version, four elders visit, and three praise Rabbi Eliezer as better for Israel than rain, the sun, and parents, but Rabbi Akiva says: 'Suffering is precious.' Rabbi Eliezer asks to be propped up to hear, and Rabbi Akiva proves it from King Menashe, whom all his father Chizkiyahu's efforts could not reform, until suffering brought him to pray and return to God.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Covers both versions of the sickbed visit back to back (Rabbah bar bar Chana's, then the four elders), ending when Rabbi Akiva's proof concludes 'suffering is precious' on 101b. The first version alone would end at 101a step 27.

items.title: Menashe appears to Rav Ashi in a dream
items.summary: Rav Ashi stopped his lesson at the three wicked kings and said: tomorrow we will begin with 'our colleagues.' King Menashe appeared to him in a dream, objected to being called a colleague, and asked him where one should begin cutting the bread for Hamotzi. Rav Ashi did not know, so Menashe taught him (from where the bread is best baked); when Rav Ashi asked why someone so wise worshipped idols, Menashe answered: 'Had you been there, you would have lifted the hem of your cloak and run after me.' The next day Rav Ashi told the Sages: we will begin with 'our teachers.'
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: "God wants the heart"
items.summary: Rabbi says that Doeg and Achitofel asked four hundred questions about 'a tower floating in the air.' Rava is not impressed: in Rav Yehuda's years they learned only Nezikin and struggled over a single Mishnah in Uktzin, while Rava's generation learns Uktzin in thirteen study halls. Yet when Rav Yehuda took off his shoes, rain came, while 'we cry out and no one pays attention to us.' The lesson: God wants the heart, as the verse says, 'and God looks at the heart.'
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Then: the nations get one easy mitzvah: the sukkah test
items.summary: The nations argue that God never forced the Torah on them the way He held the mountain over Israel at Sinai; God answers that they did not even keep the seven mitzvos they did accept. When they say Israel did not keep the Torah either, God brings witnesses from among the nations themselves, like Nimrod for Avraham and Lavan for Yaakov. They ask for the Torah again, and God says only one who prepared before Shabbos eats on Shabbos, but gives them the easy mitzvah of sukkah. Each builds a sukkah on his roof, God makes the sun blaze, each one kicks his sukkah and walks out, and God laughs at them.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Follow-on: starts right after az2a-nations ends (2b step 33). Long (39 steps) and includes a side discussion on 3a about whether non-Jews are rewarded for their mitzvos and why the sun is not 'unfair'.

items.title: Antoninus and Rabbi's secret friendship
items.summary: The Roman emperor Antoninus asks Rabbi for advice, and Rabbi answers with silent signs so the Roman nobles will not find out: a man on another's shoulders letting a dove fly (ask the Senate for one thing, and let your son do the second), and pulling up one radish a day (deal with your enemies one at a time). Antoninus sends Rabbi gold hidden under wheat, and visits him through a tunnel from his own house, killing a servant at each door so no one would know; when he once finds Rabbi Chanina bar Chama there, Rabbi Chanina brings a dead servant back to life. Antoninus serves Rabbi humbly and asks if he will reach the World to Come; Rabbi says yes, and a teaching names Antoninus and Ketiah bar Shalom as exceptions to the verses about Edom.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends just before the existing Classic az10b-ketia (10b step 19). The range also includes a coded exchange about Antoninus's daughter that the summary does not describe.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Onkelos converts and the Roman soldiers follow him
items.summary: Onkelos son of Kalonymus converted, and the emperor sent Roman soldiers to bring him back, but Onkelos drew them in with verses and they converted. The next troop was told not to say anything to him, so he told them a parable: each officer carries a torch before the one above him, yet God carries a torch before Israel ('and God went before them by day'), and they converted. The third troop was told not to talk with him at all; when he touched a mezuzah, he explained that a human king sits inside with servants guarding him outside, but God's servants sit inside and He guards them from outside. They converted too, and the emperor sent no more.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: A person only learns what his heart wants
items.summary: On the verse 'his delight is in the Torah of God', Rabbi teaches that a person can learn Torah only in an area his heart desires. Levi and Rabbi's son Rabbi Shimon were learning before Rabbi: Levi asked for Mishlei, Rabbi Shimon for Tehillim, and Tehillim was brought; when they reached this verse Rabbi taught the lesson, and Levi said, 'You have given me permission to get up.' Rabbi Avdimi bar Chama adds that God grants the wishes of one who is busy with Torah, and Rava concludes that a person should always learn where his heart desires.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's ladder
items.summary: A teaching on the verse 'guard yourself from every evil thing' warns against improper thoughts by day. From here Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair builds a ladder: Torah leads to carefulness, then eagerness, cleanliness, separation, purity, piety, humility, fear of sin, holiness, divine inspiration, and finally the revival of the dead, and piety is the greatest of all. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagrees: humility is the greatest, since the verse says the prophet was sent to bring good news 'to the humble.'
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: Why do idols sometimes "work"?
items.summary: Zunin tells Rabbi Akiva that they both know idols are nothing, yet people go to idol temples crippled and come back healed. Rabbi Akiva answers with a parable of an honest man who would not deny a deposit just because a fool forgot to bring witnesses: illnesses are sworn to leave on a set day, and they will not break their oath just because the sick person went to an idol. Rava bar Rav Yitzchak then tells Rav Yehuda of an idol that brings rain after a man is sacrificed to it, and Rav Yehuda explains that God lets the nations slip through such things to drive them from the world; as Reish Lakish says, one who comes to become impure is given an opening.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.

items.title: A court that ruled wrongly, and the people who followed it
items.summary: The Mishnah: if the beis din ruled that something the Torah forbids is allowed, and an ordinary person followed it by mistake, he is exempt because he relied on the court; but a judge who knew they erred, or a student fit to rule, who followed it anyway is liable. The Gemara asks what wording makes a real ruling, 'you are permitted' or 'you are permitted to do it', with proofs in two versions. It then asks about a man who, after the court permitted forbidden fat (chelev), mixed it up with permitted fat and ate it: Rav says he is exempt, Rabbi Yochanan says he is liable, and Rava adds that even Rav agrees he does not count toward a majority of the community.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends after the mixed-up-fat discussion, just before the Gemara turns back to the Mishnah's list of cases (2a step 30). The first question (what wording counts) is argued both ways in two versions and not formally decided.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Leadership is servitude
items.summary: A teaching excludes a king struck with tzaraas from the king's special offering, and the Gemara notes that the verse says he then lived 'in a house of freedom', which implies that until then he was a servant. The Gemara illustrates with a story: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua were traveling on a ship, and Rabbi Yehoshua had brought extra flour because of a star that rises every seventy years and misleads sailors. When Rabban Gamliel marveled at his wisdom, Rabbi Yehoshua pointed to two brilliant but poor students on land, Rabbi Elazar Chisma and Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada. Rabban Gamliel decided to appoint them, and when they came he told them: 'Do you think I am giving you power? I am giving you servitude.'

end.words: אִם הַיּוֹם תִּהְיֶה עֶבֶד לָעָם הַזֶּה״.

items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. items.title: A sin for the sake of Heaven
items.summary: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak teaches that a sin done for the sake of Heaven is greater than a mitzvah done for the wrong reason, since Yael, who sinned with Sisera, is blessed above 'the women in the tent', the Matriarchs. The Gemara objects from Rav's teaching that a person should do Torah and mitzvos even for the wrong reasons, since that leads to doing them for the right ones, so it changes the line to 'as great as.' It closes with Rav's proof: as a reward for the forty-two offerings that the wicked Balak brought, Ruth descended from him.

end.words: בֶּן בְּנוֹ שֶׁל בָּלָק מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב.

items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Separate from the 'leadership is servitude' story (see hor10a-servitude). Starts at Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak; Ulla's related line about Tamar and Zimri is the step before. The range includes frank lines about Sisera and Yael.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Anointing kings beside a spring; signs for a good year
items.summary: Kings are anointed only beside a spring, so that their rule will continue on. Rabbi Ami describes signs a person might check, like hanging a lamp between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, raising a rooster before starting a business, or looking for a shadow before a trip, but the Gemara warns against it, since a bad result can discourage a person and harm his luck. Abaye concludes that since signs do mean something, a person should get used to seeing foods like squash, fenugreek, leeks, chard and dates at the start of the year.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Ends at Abaye's Rosh Hashanah foods. The next steps (Rav Mesharshia's advice to review by a river; anointing from a horn) are loosely connected and could be added.

items.title: A scholar who is a mamzer comes before an ignorant kohen gadol
items.summary: The Mishnah ranks who comes first: kohen, Levi, Yisrael, mamzer, nasin, convert, freed slave. But this is only when they are otherwise equal: a mamzer who is a Torah scholar comes before a kohen gadol who is ignorant. The Gemara gives a reason for each step of the list, and learns the scholar's priority from the verse 'She is more precious than pearls (peninim)': Torah is more precious than the kohen gadol, who enters the innermost place (lifnai v'lifnim).
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: Who should lead: the one who knows everything, or the sharp one?
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan reports a dispute: is 'Sinai' (a scholar who knows all the teachings) better, or an 'uprooter of mountains' (a sharp reasoner)? When Rav Yosef, the 'Sinai', and Rabbah, the sharp one, were candidates to lead, the Sages of Eretz Yisrael answered that Sinai comes first, since everyone needs the owner of the wheat; yet Rav Yosef did not accept, Rabbah led for twenty-two years, and in all those years Rav Yosef did not even call a bloodletter to his house. Later Abaye became head because his statement alone was not refuted, and whether sharp Rabbi Zeira or careful Rabbah bar Rav Masna was greater is left unresolved.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav. For the rav: Starts at Rabbi Yochanan's statement on 14a. The famous story just before it (13b step 17 to 14a step 7: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Nasan try to unseat Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and are quoted as 'others' and 'some say') is a separate passage and could be its own Classic.

items.title: An offering slaughtered for the wrong purpose
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Zevachim teaches that an offering slaughtered for the sake of a different offering is still valid, but it does not count for the owner's obligation. The exceptions are the Pesach (at its proper time) and the chatas, which become invalid; Rabbi Eliezer adds the asham. The Gemara asks why the Mishnah says 'but they do not count' and answers that the animal stays holy, so the rest of the service must still be done for its proper purpose. It brings support from common sense and from the verse 'what you vowed... as a gift offering', explaining that even an offering that no longer fulfills the vow may not be changed.
items.note: Nov 2026 (Claude): new Classic. Start, end and summary read against the Gemara text; the wording awaits a rav.
items.summaryNote: summary written by Claude, not approved wording

items.title: What news did Yisro hear?
items.summary: The verse says 'Yisro heard'. The Gemara asks what news made him come and convert, and brings three answers. Rabbi Yehoshua says he heard about the war with Amalek. Rabbi Elazar HaModai says he heard about the giving of the Torah: God's voice went through the whole world, the frightened kings asked Bilam whether a new flood was coming, and Bilam told them God was giving His treasure, the Torah, to His children. Rabbi Eliezer says he heard about the splitting of the sea.

items.title: A hundred blessings a day; the three morning blessings
items.summary: Rabbi Meir taught that a person must say one hundred blessings every day, and Rav Chiya son of Rav Avya filled up the count on Shabbos and Yom Tov with blessings on spices and sweet foods. Rabbi Meir also taught three daily blessings: 'who did not make me a gentile', 'who did not make me a woman', and 'who did not make me an ignoramus'. Rav Acha bar Yaakov heard his son say the last one and objected; the son asked whether he should say 'who did not make me a slave' instead, since that seems the same as 'woman'. Rav Acha answered that a slave is lower still.

items.title: Avraham in the ruined Temple: 'What is My beloved doing in My house?'
items.summary: Rabbi Yitzchak taught that when the Temple was destroyed, God found Avraham standing in it and asked, 'What is My beloved doing in My house?' Avraham said he had come about his children. To each defense he raised (maybe they sinned by mistake, maybe only a few sinned, remember the covenant of circumcision, maybe they would have repented) God answered with a verse. Avraham put his hands on his head and wept, asking if there was no hope for them, and a heavenly voice answered that Israel is like an olive tree, whose best comes at the end.

items.title: Ben Damah wants to learn Greek wisdom
items.summary: From Rabbi Yosi's rule about the showbread (the table must never be left overnight without bread), Rabbi Ami learns that even one chapter in the morning and one in the evening fulfills 'this book of Torah shall not depart from your mouth'. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says even reciting Shema morning and evening fulfills it. Ben Damah asked his uncle Rabbi Yishmael if he, having learned the whole Torah, could study Greek wisdom; Rabbi Yishmael quoted 'you shall think about it day and night' and told him to find an hour that is neither day nor night. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yonasan disagrees, holding the verse is a blessing to Yehoshua, not a command, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael says Torah should not feel like a burden, but you may not free yourself of it.

items.title: Learning about offerings is like bringing them; 'more or less, as long as the heart is for Heaven'
items.summary: The Gemara reads the verse 'in every place offerings are presented to My name' as speaking of Torah scholars who learn anywhere: God counts it as if they brought offerings. Rabbi Yochanan says those who learn at night are like those serving in the Temple, Reish Lakish says one who learns Torah is like one who brought every kind of offering, and Rabbi Yitzchak says learning the laws of the chatas and asham is like bringing them. Then the last Mishnah of Menachot teaches that a big animal, a small bird and a flour offering are all called 'a pleasing aroma': whether one gives more or less, what matters is that his heart is directed to Heaven. Ben Azzai adds that God does not need offerings as food; they are brought for our own sake.

items.title: Who may slaughter
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Chullin says everyone may slaughter and their slaughter is valid, except a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person and a minor; if others watch them, it is valid. The Gemara asks: 'everyone may slaughter' sounds like it is allowed from the start, but 'their slaughter is valid' sounds like only after the fact. After testing whether the word 'everyone' always means 'from the start', Rabba bar Ulla explains the Mishnah: everyone may slaughter from the start, even an impure person slaughtering ordinary food kept in purity, using a long knife so he does not touch the meat. With holy offerings he should not, but if he did and is sure he did not touch the meat, it is valid.

items.title: The emperor, the lion of Bei Ilai, and the God no one can see
items.summary: Rav Yehuda identifies a giant lion 'of Bei Ilai'. The emperor mocked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: your God is compared to a lion, and a horseman can kill a lion! Rabbi Yehoshua said He is compared to the lion of Bei Ilai, and when the emperor insisted on seeing it, he prayed and it came; its roars from hundreds of parsangs away knocked down Rome's wall and the emperor from his throne, until he begged for it to be sent back. The emperor then asked to see God, and Rabbi Yehoshua showed that he could not even look at the summer sun, one of God's servants. He tried to make a feast for God, and the wind and rain, God's 'sweepers', swept it into the sea; and his daughter, who mocked God as a carpenter, was struck with leprosy, and Rabbi Yehoshua told her, 'Our God gives; He does not take back.'

items.title: The moon's complaint
items.summary: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi notes that the Torah first calls the sun and moon 'the two great lights' and then 'the great light and the small light'. The moon had said to God, 'Can two kings share one crown?', and God told her to make herself smaller. She protested, and God offered comforts: she would shine by day and night, Israel would count days and years by her, and righteous people would be called 'the small' after her. Seeing she was still not comforted, God said: bring an atonement for Me for making the moon smaller, which is why the Rosh Chodesh goat offering is called 'for God'.

items.title: 'Not because you are many': the humility of Avraham, Moshe, Aharon and David
items.summary: Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosi HaGlili, whose aggadah one should listen to closely, explains the verse 'not because you are more numerous did God desire you': God loves Israel because even when given greatness they make themselves small. Avraham said 'I am dust and ashes', Moshe and Aharon said 'what are we?', and David said 'I am a worm'. The great of the nations did the opposite: Nimrod, Pharaoh, Sancheriv, Nevuchadnetzar and Chiram became proud. The Gemara adds that the world stands because of Moshe and Aharon's humility, of one who holds himself back in a quarrel, and of one who sees himself as nothing.

items.title: The boy who fell from the ladder doing two mitzvos
items.summary: The Mishnah reasons that if the easy mitzvah of sending away the mother bird is promised long life, how much more so the weighty mitzvos. Rabbi Yaakov says every reward written in the Torah is for the World to Come: a father told his son to climb up and bring him chicks, the son sent away the mother and took the young, fulfilling both mitzvos that promise long life, yet he fell on the way down and died. The Gemara rejects other explanations (Rabbi Yaakov saw it happen; it was a rickety ladder, a known danger) and concludes that 'long days' means the world that is entirely long. Rav Yosef says that had Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) understood the verse this way, he would not have sinned.

items.title: A donkey owned with a non-Jew
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Bekhorot teaches that the firstborn-donkey law does not apply when a non-Jew has a share: if one buys the unborn foal of a non-Jew's donkey, sells his own to a non-Jew (which he should not do), is a partner with a non-Jew, or raises a donkey for one or gives his to one to raise. The verse says 'in Israel', not among others. The Gemara explains why each case is needed, then asks whether Rabbi Yehuda, who allows selling a broken animal to a non-Jew, would also allow selling an unborn one. Rav Ashi proves he would not: Rabbi Yehuda allows only an animal that cannot heal, and an unborn animal is like one that can.

items.title: 'Everyone can make an erech pledge'
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Arakhin teaches who can pledge a person's set Torah value (erech) and who can be valued: everyone, including Kohanim, Leviim, Yisraelim, women and slaves. One whose gender is unclear can pledge but cannot be valued, and a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person and a child can be valued but cannot pledge, since they lack understanding. The Gemara asks what each 'everyone' in the Mishnah adds: a sharp child close to adulthood can pledge, a disfigured or boil-covered person can be valued, and a baby under a month can be the subject of a vow of worth.

items.title: The spies and the power of lashon hara
items.summary: The Mishnah teaches that a man who falsely spreads a bad name about his wife pays a hundred sela, more than one who actually violates a girl, so speech is treated more harshly than action; the decree against the desert generation was sealed only because of the spies' evil report. The Gemara proves that the fine is for the bad name itself, and that 'they tested Me this ten times' shows the decree was sealed for this sin. Rabbi Elazar ben Parta says: if the spies were punished so for speaking badly about wood and stones, how much more so one who speaks badly about his friend. Reish Lakish proves they died for their report about the land.

items.title: Who in this generation knows how to rebuke?
items.summary: A baraita teaches that 'do not hate your brother in your heart' means hidden hatred, that one must rebuke a friend who does wrong, even again and again, but never to the point of embarrassing him. Rabbi Tarfon wondered whether anyone in his generation could accept rebuke, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya whether anyone knew how to give it; Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri said that his complaints about Rabbi Akiva only made Rabbi Akiva love him more. Rav Huna would not rebuke Chiya bar Rav to his face so as not to embarrass Rav's son. The Gemara ends with how far rebuke must go: until he hits, curses or scolds you.

items.title: Who can make a substitution
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Temurah says everyone can substitute an animal for a consecrated one, men and women alike; not that it is allowed, but if one does, it takes effect and he receives lashes. The Gemara asks how 'everyone substitutes' fits with 'not that it is allowed', and Rav Yehuda explains: everyone has the power to make the holiness take hold. 'Everyone' includes an heir, against Rabbi Yehuda, who holds an heir can neither lean on the offering (semichah) nor make a substitution. The Gemara traces each side to its verses, including how 'and if he shall substitute' teaches that a woman can substitute.

items.title: The thirty-six sins that carry kareis
items.summary: The first Mishnah of Keritot lists the thirty-six sins in the Torah that carry kareis: forbidden relations, blasphemy, idol worship, Molech, Shabbos desecration, eating forbidden fats, blood and leftover offerings, chametz on Pesach, eating or working on Yom Kippur, misusing the anointing oil or incense, and failing to bring the Pesach or to circumcise. For these, doing it on purpose brings kareis, by mistake a chatas, and in doubt an asham talui, except for one who makes the Temple impure (Rabbi Meir) and, say the Sages, the blasphemer. The Gemara asks why the Mishnah gives a number, and Rabbi Yochanan answers: one who did them all in one lapse must bring a separate offering for each, and the same is true of the thirty-nine labors of Shabbos.

items.title: The foul-smelling chelbenah: a fast must include the sinners
items.summary: Rabbi Shimon Chasida taught that any fast that does not include some of the sinners of Israel is not a fast, because chelbenah (galbanum) smells bad, yet the Torah counts it among the spices of the incense. Abaye learns the same idea from the verse 'He established His bundle on the earth': Israel is one bundle.

items.title: Then: Alexander at the gates of Gan Eden, and the eye that is never satisfied
items.summary: Alexander told the Elders of the Negev he wanted to go to Africa, and they advised him to bring donkeys that walk in the dark and ropes to find his way back. He reached a town of women, who talked him out of war and served him bread of gold, mocking his greed; he wrote on the gate that he had learned good sense from women. At a spring whose fragrance came from Gan Eden, he followed it to the gate and was refused, and was given an eyeball that outweighed all his gold and silver. The Rabbis explained it was the human eye, which is never satisfied, and proved it: when they covered it with dust it was weighed down at once.

items.title: The angel at conception: 'strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor'
items.summary: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish learn the rule that marital relations should be at night from different verses. Reish Lakish uses Iyov's verse 'the night that said: a man is conceived' for Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's teaching: the angel in charge of conception is named 'Night'; he takes the drop before God and asks whether it will be strong or weak, wise or foolish, rich or poor. But he does not ask whether it will be righteous or wicked, because, as Rabbi Chanina said, everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven.

items.title: Three partners in every person
items.summary: A baraita teaches that every person has three partners: God, the father and the mother. The father and mother provide the body, and God gives the spirit and soul, the face's features, sight, hearing, speech, walking, understanding and wisdom. When a person's time comes to leave the world, God takes His share and leaves the parents' share before them, which Rav Pappa compares to the saying 'shake off the salt and throw the meat to the dog'.

items.title: 'Whoever learns halachos every day': the end of Shas
items.summary: The last teaching of the Talmud, from the school of Eliyahu: whoever learns halachos every day is promised a place in the World to Come, as the verse says 'halichos olam lo', the ways of the world are his. Do not read it halichos, ways, but halachos, laws. Then the closing words of Niddah, and of the whole Shas.
